title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) False Start
summary: This informational RFC specifies an optional TLS client behavior called False Start. It affects only timing, not the on-the-wire data, can be implemented unilaterally, and reduces handshake latency to one round trip.

plainLanguage.summary: The client starts sending real data a bit early, before finishing the handshake, saving a round trip.

questions: how to reduce tls handshake latency
subtitle: Let a TLS client send application data one round trip sooner, but only when strict safety conditions hold.

tldr.problem: A full TLS handshake up to TLS 1.2 needs two rounds before data can flow, adding two round-trip times for protocols where the client speaks first, such as HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: The client may send application data right after its own ChangeCipherSpec and Finished messages, before the server's, if it uses only whitelisted ciphers, versions and key exchanges.
tldr.outcome: This keeps the added latency to one round trip. The RFC puts security restrictions on when it is allowed, because the handshake is not yet validated.

today: RFC 7918 is Informational, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The text says False Start will not be needed with TLS 1.3 and later, since fewer round trips is a first-order design goal there.

sections.title: The Latency Problem
sections.content:
A full TLS handshake in versions up to TLS 1.2 takes two protocol rounds (four flights) before application data can be sent. For protocols where the client sends first, like HTTP, that adds two network round-trip times. False Start lets the client send data when the handshake is only partly done, after it has sent its own ChangeCipherSpec and Finished but before it receives the server's. The added latency drops to one round trip.

If the handshake later completes, it is validated retroactively and the traffic looks normal apart from timing. If it fails, an attacker may have tampered with handshake messages, and data was sent that otherwise would not have been. That risk is why the RFC restricts when False Start is allowed.

Abbreviated handshakes (session resumption) do not need a client-side False Start, and the RFC does not consider server-side False Start further. TLS 1.3 and later are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting for two 'ready' replies makes you slow. If everything checks out, you can start after just one.

sections.title: False Start Compatibility
sections.content:
False Start is optional. A server is False Start compatible if it tolerates receiving TLS records early, before the protocol is ready to process them. A client can only use False Start successfully with such a server.

Appendix A explains that typical implementations are compatible without knowing about False Start: thanks to transport layer buffering, early application data records just remain buffered until the server has sent its own Finished message.
sections.plainLanguage: The listener has to be fine with getting a message a little early and keeping it until ready.

sections.title: Client-Side False Start
sections.content:
By default a client waits for the server's ChangeCipherSpec and Finished before sending data. With False Start, the client MAY send application data earlier, under the new Cipher Spec, if all of these hold:

  • The application layer requested False Start.
  • The symmetric cipher has been whitelisted.
  • The protocol version in ServerHello.server_version has been whitelisted.
  • The key exchange method and its parameters have been whitelisted.
  • With client authentication, the client certificate type has been whitelisted.

Rules for receiving data are unchanged. Being able to send data does not mean an authenticated peer is present, so implementations should let the application ask whether the handshake has completed.
sections.plainLanguage: You may start early only if you tick every box on a safety list.

sections.title: Why the Restrictions Exist
sections.content:
In TLS the Finished messages validate the whole handshake, so an attacker who altered it, for example to force a weaker cipher suite, cannot produce a valid Finished. False Start gives up some of this: data may be sent before the handshake is confirmed, so there is generally no way to be sure the expected peer is present.

The goal is therefore that if anyone at all can decrypt the False Start data, it must be the legitimate peer. The RFC also says it is prudent for applications to be even more restrictive, for instance skipping False Start for handshakes that do not match the common pattern.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting early means you cannot yet be sure who is listening. So you only do it when even a sneaky listener could not read what you send.

sections.title: Ciphers, Versions and Key Exchange
sections.content:
Clients MUST NOT use False Start unless the cipher is considered cryptographically strong, generally an effective key length of 128 bits or more. AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and AES_256_GCM_SHA384 are called sufficiently strong for most uses, while none of the ciphers in RFC 4492 and RFC 5246 can be recommended. Implementations should whitelist generally only their highest supported protocol version, to avoid downgrade attacks.

The recommended key exchange whitelist is DHE_RSA, ECDHE_RSA, DHE_DSS and ECDHE_ECDSA, with well-known DH groups of at least 3,072 bits or named curves of at least 256 bits, and the client certificate type none. These choices mean no False Start happens if the handshake would lack forward secrecy.
sections.plainLanguage: Only start early when the lock is strong, the rules are the newest ones, and the key swap protects past messages even if a secret leaks later.
